summary: Instagram is where almost all the audience is: most Hindi videos get 500 to 1,400 views there, while YouTube Shorts mostly get under 60 views. The best performers use a surprising 'X doesn't do what you think, it only does Y' hook about a familiar sensor or gadget. Shares are rare but powerful: the UV sunburn and soil sensor videos got 33 and 24 shares from small view counts, while generic 'How does X work?' titles and the YouTube-only uploads got almost nothing.
winningPattern: Instagram-first Hindi Shorts about one familiar sensor or everyday gadget, with a myth-busting title in the form 'X doesn't do [obvious thing], it only does [surprising thing]' (e.g. 'Clap Switch Taali Nahi, Sirf Shor Sunta Hai', 'DHT11 Aag Nahi Dekhta, Sirf Garmi Pakadta Hai'). Robots and clap-switch topics get the most saves and views. Surprising real-life facts such as sunburn on cloudy days get the most shares. Titles are short, use one emoji, and are posted on both platforms. The 'How does X work? 🤔' question format flopped.
doMore: Use the 'X doesn't do A, it only does B' myth-bust title and on-screen hook on every video
Post every video to Instagram Reels first, as it brings 10 to 50 times more views than YouTube
Make more robot and clap-switch style videos (robot falling without gyro, line follower, seeti on clap switch) since they get the most views and saves
Pick topics tied to a real-life surprise (cloudy-day sunburn, soil moisture, breathalyzer) and end with a line that invites sharing, like 'send this to a friend who thinks...'
Test the YouTube side with a stronger first-second visual and a clear keyword title, because it gets very little now
stopDoing: Generic 'Kaise kaam karta hai? 🤔' question titles
Uploading to YouTube only, with no Instagram post (about 12 videos got zero Instagram reach)
Making several near-duplicate videos on the same topic (PIR, IR, clap switch, tap) without a new angle
